newsitem.title: USA: AIDS drug therapy should begin earlier - panel.
newsitem.headline: AIDS drug therapy should begin earlier - panel.

text.p: People infected with HIV should begin aggressive drug therapy earlier and not just when the signs of AIDS appear, a panel of experts said Tuesday.

"New data have provided a stronger rationale for earlier initiation of more aggressive therapy than previously recommended," Charles Carpenter, chairman of the International AIDS Society-USA panel, wrote in a report. Carpenter is a doctor at Brown University School of Medicine in Providence, Rhode Island.
Previous recommendations for therapy have been based on the HIV patient's symptoms, higher levels of the replicating virus in the body and a decline in immune system cells in the blood.

Patients must be committed to a "lifelong adherence to the necessary treatment," which can be costly, complex and potentially toxic, the panel wrote in the Journal of the American Medical Association.
"One must be especially careful not to prematurely abandon a given regimen shortly after the initiation of therapy," it said.

The most effective therapy against the deadly virus has proven to be a "drug cocktail" consisting of two nucleoside analog reverse transcriptase inhibitors, including zidovudine (AZT), and one protease inhibitor, the report said.
